Backyard putting greens for Longwood lots

A backyard putting green in Longwood runs $14–$30 a square foot, typically $18–$25, as of September 2026. A contoured green never needs irrigation in the first place, which means it sits entirely outside the watering-day schedule that governs the rest of a Longwood yard, inside city limits or in one of the unincorporated pockets around it.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A green that never touches the watering schedule

Longwood's own water utility follows the Seminole County odd-and-even schedule: odd addresses Wednesday and Saturday, even addresses Thursday and Sunday, nothing between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. A putting green was never part of that math to begin with, since synthetic turf on a contoured green needs a hose rinse for dust and pollen, not a sprinkler zone, so the household's watering days keep applying to whatever lawn surrounds it rather than to the green itself.

Keeping a green's base off the septic drainfield

A Longwood yard with a septic system needs its drainfield and pump-out lid located before staking a putting green's tiers, since the deeper four- to six-inch excavation a green requires disturbs more ground than a flat lawn conversion does, and the state's rule still requires that lid stay reachable once the green is finished. A green's shaped contours make working around a fixed access point harder than it would be on open lawn, so the design usually routes tiers and cup locations away from that spot entirely rather than trying to shape a break around it. This gets settled before any digging starts.

Grading a contour into a lot platted decades ago

A number of Longwood's established subdivisions were graded for drainage long before anyone planned a putting green on the lot, which means the yard's existing high and low points often become the starting contour rather than something built from scratch. A green tucked into a natural swale in the corner of an older yard can borrow that existing fall for a subtle break, while a flatter section closer to the house usually needs its own shaped subbase to get any roll at all.

What stimp speed actually depends on

Ball roll speed on a Longwood putting green, measured on a stimpmeter, comes from a combination of fiber type, infill, and grooming rather than any single spec on a product sheet, which is why two greens built with the same nylon can still stimp differently. Home installations generally land somewhere in the eight to thirteen range depending on that combination, with nylon and a lighter, more even infill layer typically producing a faster, more consistent roll than a heavier infill or a less groomed surface. Asking for a stimp reading on an installer's own finished work says more than a manufacturer's brochure number ever will.

Say you have a corner of the backyard for a green

Say you have a 480 sq ft green with fringe planned for the back corner of an established Longwood lot, far enough from the house to avoid the low-E glass on a rear sliding door. At $14–$30 a square foot, that runs $6,720 to $14,400, and at the more typical $18–$25, most quotes land between $8,640 and $12,000. A single cup and a gentle two-tier break keep the shaping simple, and because the green sits well clear of any drip line on this lot, the full 480 sq ft stays buildable rather than shrinking once a tree canopy gets factored in.

Seaming the putting surface and fringe as separate pieces

The short putting surface and the taller fringe turf around a Longwood green get cut and seamed as two distinct pieces rather than one continuous roll, since they're different products at different pile heights doing different jobs. That seam is placed deliberately along the design's edge line so it reads as a mowing transition once grooming is finished, not as a visible patch where two products meet. Getting this seam line right the first time matters more on a green than on a lawn, since the edge is exactly where a chip shot lands and a rough transition is the most visible spot on the entire surface.

When a base is shaped for looks instead of drainage

A Longwood green built by someone chasing dramatic breaks without matching drainage capacity in the low points will look impressive on a dry day and pond badly after the first real storm, since water collects in exactly the tiers designed to be most visually interesting. Standing water sitting in a low tier softens that part of the base well before the rest of the green shows any wear, and the surface above it stops rolling the way it was designed to soon after, sometimes within a single rainy season. Shaping decisions and drainage planning have to happen together from the start, not as a layer added on top of an afterthought base.

Fringe, cups and a lawn built around a much older canopy

On a lot with a mature oak within reach of where a green would sit, the drip-line rule shapes the layout before the contour does, since the fringe and the green itself both count as turf under that setback. A crew planning a green near Casselberry-style established canopy, or anywhere else in Longwood with decades-old trees, checks the drip line first and designs the hole placement and fringe width around whatever space is left. Contour shaping and cup placement work the same everywhere; the general putting-green guide has the fringe and turf-pile specifics this page doesn't repeat.

Brushing a green to keep the roll consistent

Consistency in a Longwood green's roll comes far more from regular grooming than from the age of the surface itself, which is why a light pass with a stiff brush, moving opposite the nap direction, belongs on a repeating schedule rather than a once-a-year task. Skipping several months between brushings lets the fiber settle into whatever direction foot traffic and rain have pushed it, and a ball crossing that section starts to pull slightly off line even though nothing about the green looks different to the eye. A gentle, frequent touch keeps the surface predictable in a way that one thorough grooming a year never quite manages.

Questions people ask

Does a putting green in Longwood need irrigation heads capped like a lawn does?

Only if heads already exist under where the green will sit. A green typically replaces grass that was already being watered, so any head in that footprint gets capped the same way it would for a full lawn conversion, per the state's turf standard.

Can a putting green go inside Longwood's historic district?

Nothing published treats a putting green differently from any other synthetic-turf project inside the district's roughly 190 acres, so the same design-review question that applies to a full lawn applies here if the green would be visible from the street.

Do Longwood's older lots have enough flat space for a green?

Often yes, since many were platted with a rear lawn deep enough for one, but a lot heavy with mature oak canopy may only offer a smaller, shadier footprint than a newer subdivision would.
